The remainder of the valid Perl programs are mostly valid due to a Perl
  language feature that is not commonly present in most programming languages.
  Namely, Perl has a feature called “unquoted strings”, in which a sequence
  of alphanumeric characters by itself is parsed as though it were a quoted string.
  As an example, Figure 5 is read by OCR as the text ME, which evaluates to the
  string “ME” even though the ME isn’t quoted. This would result in a syntax
  error in most other programming languages.

  (To be fair to Perl, when perl is run with the -w flag to enable warnings, it does
  helpfully inform the user that at some point in the future, the Perl developers
  will most likely pick gggijgziifiiffif as a new reserved word:
      Unquoted string "gggijgziifiiffif" may clash
      with future reserved word at - line 1.)reply
first_paragraph: Posted 2019-04-01.TLDR: read the paper and view the gallery of pretty Perl programs.In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl?We answer this question in the affirmative: it is possible to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs.Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand we’ve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.”R

first_paragraph: I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15.It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that.Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing.Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink>) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”.At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems,

first_paragraph: AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs.AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS.The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead.AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. title: Gemini Decisions API (blog.google)
comments: I'm sort of surprised it took Jev for everyone to realize "oh yeah, this is a useful thing that we should have in our product portfolio".But maybe this is one of those things that's only obvious in retrospect?  I'm sure people were trying something similar years ago with grammar-constrained outputs (for example to only output a simple json structure), but you can't get probabilities out of the model that way.   Which makes me wonder:  how do these models calculate probabilities?reply

A lot of AI stuff is like that, actually. GPT 2 and 3 were mainly curiosities that would get articles on tech news sites but didn’t attract much attention from the general public. But after RLHF the UX improved dramatically and ChatGPT became mainstream. A lot of MLEs underestimate how much UX matters, and the same is true for Jev.> how do these models calculate probabilities?The short answer is: more and better data.The long answer is: probably the same way any other classifier does. Take your ground truth probabilities and your predicted probabilities. The gap between those is called cross entropy, which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.reply

> which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.The definition of "correct probability" here is usually "p=1 for the ground truth label, p=0 for all others." Which seems like an intuitive approach but if you actually think about it doesn't trivially imply the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty.reply

For a single prediction, sure. But the model doesn't make a single prediction and then stop existing. It makes an unbounded number of future predictions and under that assumption it is reasonable to expect the model to behave optimally under Bayes rule - which has a unique global minimizer at E[(Y-F(X))^2].So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.reply

title: Lock Your GitHub Actions (hugovk.dev)
comments: The advice here is really great (as I'd expect from Hugo), but as the maintainer of zizmor I want to note some caveats with the current iteration of workflow lockfiles:- They only lock normal action calls. If your workflows invoke other reusable workflows, you need to keep those hash-pinned manually for now.- Composite actions are not themselves locked. Instead, they get locked transitively through their callsites i.e. the workflows that call them. This makes any individual caller that uses lockfiles safe, but it also makes the current `gh actions-lock` default unsafe (since it removes hash-pins from the composite action itself, meaning that any external caller that invokes the action loses their transitive pinning).- Other forms of `uses:` clauses, like Docker images, are also not currently locked via the lockfile. And the same for forms of interior mutability (like an action running `npx ...` under the hood, although the latter is fully outside of GitHub's control to prevent. But these mean that you can't assume that a fully locked Actions setup is in fact 100% immutable.I hope they address these gaps soon, because it's otherwise an excellent (and long-awaited) feature.reply

comments: The hardest part of the transition from prebiotic chemistry (assembling the building blocks) to an 'RNA World' is doing so in a way that can support RNA copying. As others have shown the chance of finding one replicator is low - so you need supporting RNA copying chemistry at a pretty substantial level to help that happen.This is where the hard part of the field is currently: finding chemistry that can support accurate RNA copying that is also both sufficiently high yielding and also compatible with these reactions being inside protocells (fatty acids for example). An RNA genome only really has value when it can be selfish and keep any innovations it makes to itself inside a protocell!I work in Origins Research - if you have questions please ask and ill try to answer with the current opinions of the field!reply

The actual knowledge encoded in the RNA sequence—not the physical stuff; but the precise coded sequence—required for replication is actually quite ubiquitous across species and unchanged on timescales vastly larger than I had previously fathomed, mountains look like sand castles and sharks are brand new in the eyes of the code of RNA. This is only an analogy; but it felt like how Unix works: RNA is like the tiny kernel which has spread everywhere due to being tiny and good enough to solve the problem and therefore difficult to replace. Has the precise RNA code survived a really long time and it’s sort of like an old operating system which just keeps humming in the background? And it is older than sharks right? > what’s the actual problem?A combinatorial explosion. To have mutations you need to have replication first. If a smallest viable self-replicator is, say, 100 nucleotides long, and there's not many other such replicators of the same length, the improbability of its spontaneous formation (~4^-100) dwarfs any amount of material available on Earth.The researchers have found QT45 replicator. But it replicates other RNA strands, that is it needs another replicator nearby to replicate itself, which brings the probability down to 4^-90 range.And it's not clear from the article whether QT45 is a viable replicator. That is whether it is stable enough and replicates other RNA strands correctly enough to sustain exponential growth instead of petering out due to filling its surroundings with broken copies that don't perform replication before decaying itself.reply

I doubt a replicator came out of thin air. It seems more likely, at least to me, that we started with constructors, that created primitive sequences.Imagine you have molecules that can form spontaneously, like gliders in Conway's Game of Life. You may have several different molecules that are capable of helping to create one another -- an autocatalytic set.Eventually this could result in more complex chains, and eventually a self replicating molecule can arise.Imagine slamming a bunch of gliders together to make a machine that replicates more gliders. It's possible! Not likely, but there are so many variables that can influence the environment substantially. It's not like there was a giant homogeneous soup. Parts from over here and over there would form differently and when they meet, amazing things can happen.In the Game of Life, this spontaneous event is extremely unlikely, astronomically unlikely.Unlike Game of Life, the real world has a few advantages that improve performance. For one, it's less fragile. Bonds are much stronger and collisions don't cause everything to break. Another advantage is that bonds are attractive: molecules can rotate and turn to snap together strongly. Gliders just explode violently. And finally, the real world is very dense. We're talking trillions of molecules mixing around millions of times per second per microdroplet. Compound that with a few hundred million years... it certainly doesn't feel as surprising as you might expect.If there were a highly advanced alien race watching earth over a long period of time, it might be interesting, but not unexpected, that suddenly an Eiffel tower springs forth from the surface of the planet, erected by intelligent organisms.reply

The simple combinatorial explosion criticism feels reductive to me.  It's exceedingly unlikely that a single "self-replicating RNA molecule" formed independently by chance and then propagated.Let's say that you have some RNA soup with some ribozymes some of which weakly encourage some reaction involving other RNA molecules.  The occurrence of a cycle of reinforcing reactions might be sufficient to build a crude evolutionary ratchet.In fact the "cycle of reactions" perspective feels a bit more robust to me since it allows for the proto-replication process to take place over a longer period of time and over larger areas.reply

title: How to make a CNC plasma cutter with high-frequency start (incoherency.co.uk)
comments: What you all think about this one - https://youtu.be/wX-ivETq0nw ?reply

Nice build. There's been a lot of momentum in the desktop wire EDM community too, with projects like picoEDM, Gedm, openEDM, and baxEDM. Precision is the usual weakness of plasma cutting, but I suppose it makes up for that in speed. Have you tried tuning for kerf width or taper, or is that more trouble than it's worth at this scale?reply

Potentially easier solution for the USB problem: measure your cables with a DMM until you find one with good end-to-end shield continuity.  A large proportion of USB cables have no effective common-mode protection (to say nothing of EMI shielding) because one end or both ends is ungrounded.reply

Tying the grounds of multiple devices together over USB cables is likely to create a ground loop. Grounding is supposed to be a tree, rooted at the stake in the ground out by the electric meter. If you don't have that, every loop becomes an antenna.
That's why braids are usually grounded only at one end.This matters when you have something as RF noisy as a plasma cutter nearby.If you have a scope, you can start looking at signals to see where there's RF hash.
Then you can try putting ferrite inductors around various power and data cables to
see if it helps. Often it does.There are USB opto isolator cables.I'd really like to see a big red switch on that setup to turn everything off. If somebody like a first responder ever needs to shut that thing off, it's not at all obvious which plug to pull first.(I used to use the rather antiquated plasma cutter at the original TechShop. It never started properly. Plasma cutters start by creating an arc between electrode and the nearby nozzle. That makes some plasma, which is then blown out to the workpiece. Once there's plasma from electrode to workpiece, the nozzle is cut out of circuit. The one at TechShop had a consumable copper electrode and a consumable copper nozzle cap. The electrode is supposed to get all the wear, because the nozzle cap is only involved when the arc starts. TechShop's machine often failed to cut the nozzle cap out of circuit, and it consumed nozzle caps faster than electrodes. TechShop sold nozzle caps.)reply

I do this stuff for a living, and have an enormous amount of experience with it.  There are worse things than ground loops, and USB cables with broken shields are one of them.  Braids in sensitive applications are essentially never grounded at only one end.Ferrites do nothing for low-frequency impulse noise, which is what this type of issue usually comes down to.  They are there to pass FCC/CE tests, and that's it.  Optically-isolated cables can indeed be a good solution, but not many of them support USB 2.0 HS unfortunately (which my stuff needs).  Might be the right answer here.reply

I got noise out of 5V TTL encoder signals with clamp-around ferrites around the motor power leads. The encoder input was picking up the servomotor power.The big problem here is that you can't do much about the source. A plasma arc started with audio-frequency AC (10KHz?) is going to emit RF. Not clear what the waveform looks like. If it's a square wave, which it probably is, there will be higher harmonics. Fortunately, it's only AC only during start; the cutter shifts to DC once the arc has been struck. Otherwise those things would be a huge interference headache whenever they were on.reply

slag, cut taper, leadins and warping affecting surface level are all constant annoyances with plasma. I find it a lot easier to just send jobs to a waterjet shop nearby.my friend did a lot of bulk plasma cutting, and his solution was to build a tumbler filled with abrasive and dish soap, and after a day or so the edges would be smooth and rounded. but that's certainly not a replacement for machined parts.reply
first_paragraph:
The issue with high-frequency start ("HF start") on plasma cutters is that igniting the pilot arc creates an enormous
amount of electromagnetic interference which causes problems for nearby electronics, in particular tending to disconnect
the USB connection to your CNC motion controller. You can solve this by talking to the motion controller over WiFi.This is my machine in its temporary location on the workbench:If you still need to acquire a plasma cutter then I obviously recommend trying to get one with "blowback start" instead of "HF start"
so that you don't have to worry about it. In acquiring a machine with HF start I made an error. But I got it to work anyway,
so if you already have an HF start machine and you want to use it for CNC, you might be able to do the same thing.I kind of wanted a CNC plasma cutter because I have recently spent lots of time and end mills making planar parts like this for my cyclecar

first_paragraph: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAGMaximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically.
